citations.review_text: Great game would highly recommend good for solo and mutli player play

I recommend Slay the Spire 2 to every TCG fan 👍 This type of game is even more fun when you can enjoy it with a friend.

The quintessential deck-building roguelike gets a sequel... With multiplayer!

Slay The Spire 2 is quite fun to explore and experiment with, even in early access. Five unique characters each with various mechanics and playstyles, and 11 difficulty levels to work through; this means a lot of time to learn your characters (and learn how to mitigate questionable card rewards).

The game isn't perfect. Some runs are seemingly unwinnable, and many builds are just statistically less viable than others. The game periodically sandbags your deck with zero synergy or low-efficacy cards, and will often throw enemies at you that outright counter whichever character/build you've assembled, bringing runs to an early end. It's forgivable to a degree though, given the nature of the game; unlocking more cards/relics to give it another go or swapping characters to try a different approach on a new run will usually help break up the frustration.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the character animations and visual fidelity as an improvement over the original game.

citations.review_text: More of what made the original Slay The Spire amazing, the additional visuals make it more amazing!

Slay the Spire 2 is the sequel to Slay the Spire, a game that gave us the roguelike deckbuilding genre as we know today. Fundamentally, it's a simple game where you ascend the spire to reach the final boss, all while collecting cards to build your deck and slowly become more powerful. The sequel doesn't make too many changes to the fundamentals of the game, but it adds just enough to feel fresh while also being what I believe to be the best game I've played this year.

In terms of presentation, it is a step up from the original Slay the Spire in some interesting ways, and in others needs improvement. The character designs for the main cast of playable characters are improved in terms of fidelity, and the added animations are a serviceable addition despite some clear roughness and repeated usage, though some characters I feel need to have a more distinct design. An example is the Ironclad: it is a better design fidelity-wise compared to the original, but the original has a more distinct design overall. However, that is not to say the character designs are bad; on the contrary, they are great and more lively, which speaks to the improved art direction of the game. The art for the cards as well are incredible, and the card designs remain clean so that information is made more clear. My favorite of the card designs are the ones where the art takes up the entire card; they're unique and beautiful in design.

Music and sound in Slay the Spire 2 is also fairly good. The dramatic, orchestra-esque soundtrack compliments the fantastical DnD-esque nature of the game's systems and world, and there were moments when fighting bosses where the music peaks with a dramatic flare, such as when a boss is doing its most powerful attack. The sound design for every card played and every attack performed is simple but effective, perfectly complimenting the systems at play and giving every action substantial impact.

citations.review_text: This game is peak, in order to play it at its best you will need 3 friends to do a 4 man run, it is then that the game truly shines but I would still say 9.5/10 even when playedd alone

The dev team carried over all the good parts of the first game and then added even more. The devs are giving this game a ton of support through early access and the love that they have for the game shows through clearly. This is the GOAT of deck building roguelikes, and acts as the gold standard by which all others are judged. 

The multiplayer aspect of this game is amazing. Being able to play with anywhere from 1 to 4 people is absolutely fantastic and some of the most fun I've had in ages. My only hope is that couch coop gets added in at some point.

STS1 has a very special place in my heart and when the early access for STS2 was released, I knew I had to pick this up. Adding co-op to this game and playing with friends brings a whole new perspective into the game and feels like a breath of fresh air. Not only can my friends experience rage inducing moments with me, but we get the chance to collaborate on new builds that are different every time. Lately, I've been enjoying custom mode with 3-4 players since we have beaten all 10 ascensions. I appreciate the hard work the devs have been putting into this, and while I miss the weekly/biweekly updates, I know they are working hard.

A few critiques I've had in multiplayer:
I find the game becomes exponentially easier as soon as 3 players (or a team of four) are added. The game becomes more of a challenge at 2 players, but has slightly become easier with the addition of the Ball card. On a more positive note, I've really enjoyed playing support with mutliplayer cards. Giving all allies block and energy really can turn my Ironclad runs from  high DPS to full on support. Also, thanks for allowing us to Doodle on the maps, I love seeing the artwork every Neowsletter, and it makes my runs go alot faster when I can just draw what path I want. Also, please more colours for multiplayer! It makes players who choose the same character who doodle sad when we can't tell apart ://

While playing with friends, I feel like Doom builds always seem to fall off. Its so much easier to pick the Silent and go the classic Shiv/Poison Route. Osty builds have been much more accessible/ common playing with friends, and Doom builds just can't keep up unless other players also commit to the same build during the Run.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as featuring active beta branch updates during its early access period.

citations.review_text: I am old. 42 as of writing this. I've been playing games since 1990 and have experienced just about everything in the medium. STS2 is without question my personal favorite game of all time and it's not even finished yet. I was there at the beginning of both StS games, following them through the beta branch iterations experiencing the tuning get dialed in as we head to 1.0 is just so amazing to watch as a gaming lifer. I just completed my first rotating 5-streak on ascension 10 (no act 4 yet though..) and now am moving to the just released dread mode. Can't get enough. Mega Crit are legendary devs. Any pissy reviews are short sighted, this is the apex of the genre.

I thought this game was just one or two small steps away from perfection.
But the devs decided to take a leap up the Spire.

---

TL;DR: An already incredible game just received its most ambitious beta update yet. The developers keep listening, the gameplay keeps evolving, and somehow, this sequel has already begun surpassing its genre-defining predecessor. I genuinely believe we're witnessing another landmark in roguelike deckbuilding, one that could reshape the genre all over again. The future of this masterpiece-in-the-making looks absurdly bright, and we haven't even reached 1.0.

10/10. Would climb again.

---

⚠️ BETA BRANCH SPOILERS AHEAD! (Stop here for the spoiler-free verdict.)

Slay the Spire 2 was incredible from day one. I loved it, poured hundreds of hours into it, but still had that nagging feeling that something was missing before I could confidently call it a 10/10 like its predecessor.

Then v0.113.0 arrived (still exclusive to the beta branch at the time of this review), and apparently the developers decided that small improvements weren't enough.

Every update since launch has brought something worthwhile to the table. The developers have genuinely listened to every corner of their community, from beginners struggling to reach Act 2 to elite players who calculate survival probabilities, plan lethal draws several turns ahead, and squeeze every last drop of value from their resources (some pros are so terrifyingly consistent, even at A10, that I occasionally wonder if we're even playing the same game).

Over the months, we've watched everything from tiny numerical adjustments to sweeping card reworks and even entire boss replacements. Events have become more interesting, synergies more satisfying, and countless little interactions more intuitive. All that work has gradually shaped a game with extraordinary strategic depth, where there's always something new to discover and another level of mastery to pursue.

And now comes v0.113.0, the biggest bet…

single_points.text: One reviewer says that the Entomancer punishes you for spamming low damage attacks by shuffling dazed cards into your draw pile.

citation.review_text:
A really great card game, which receives a lot of misguided criticism.

The design philosophy of enemies in sts2 is quite interesting. Unlike its predecessor, a lot of enemies demand an immediate answer to their mechanics, otherwise you get hopelessly crushed. A good example is the Entomancer; it punishes you for spamming low damage attacks by shuffling dazed cards into your draw pile. It [i]demands[/i] the player to play big damage attacks or apply damage without directly attacking it. 

Here is where a lot of frustration begins for a lot of players. They feel like these fights are unfair because the deck archetype that they just so happen to build around is completely countered by the enemy. Had they not encountered it, they would have been better off. Combine this with the fact that these enemies keep getting buffed (and certain card synergies nerfed), and you have people that complain.

The thing is that humans are [u]really[/u] bad at understanding when something was bad luck or an accumulation of many small mistakes. It's not obvious why you die in this game, so its easy to blame the 'poor' balancing rather than recognising that you made some bad choices. 

When I started to take my time to think through my options and learn from my past mistakes, the game became so much more fun and creative. I've won A10 runs with exotic decks where cards that are seen as typically bad performed well in my deck. I do not think about which cards fit an archetype that I'm playing, because I completely avoid them; I think about which cards my deck needs to solve future problems. Sometimes that means picking niche cards. 

This is the beauty of the game: instead of being forced into always picking S-tier cards that fit an 'archetype', lower-tier cards are sometimes the optimal choice. Spotting that and seeing it play out well is super satisfying. I think the game is heading in the right direction. Every patch makes me enjoy the game even more and I hope that they will continue t…
